chunks: As for what Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā narrated from ʿAlī ibn Ḥadīd, from some of our companions, who said:

I was with Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام on the road to Makkah. We came to a well, and the servant of Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام drew up a bucket, and two mice came out in it. So Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: “Pour it out.” Then he drew another, and a mouse came out in it, so Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام said: “Pour it out.” Then he drew a third, and nothing came out in it, so he said: “Pour it into the vessel.” So he poured it into the vessel.

So the first thing about this report is that it is mursal, and its narrator is weak, namely ʿAlī ibn Ḥadīd; and this weakens using his report as proof. And even if it is accepted, it is possible that what is meant by the well is a reservoir in which there is an amount of water exceeding the measure of a kurr, so no water needs to be drawn out from it; and that is what is customary on the road to Makkah. Moreover, there is nothing in the report stating that he performed wudu (ablution) with that water; rather, he said to his servant: “Pour it into the vessel,” and in that there is no proof for the permissibility of using water of this ruling-status in wudu (ablution). It is also possible that he only ordered him to pour it into the vessel because they needed it for watering beasts and camels, or for drinking in a state of necessity requiring it, and that is permissible. It is also possible that the two mice came out alive, and if that was so, then using what remained of the water is permissible, because that does not render the water najis, as has preceded earlier. And what further clarifies it is what...

key_terms.الْكُرِّ: the legal measure of abundant water affecting rulings of purity
key_terms.الْوُضُوءِ: wudu (ablution), the ritual purification whose permissibility is being evaluated
key_terms.بِئْرٍ: a well, the source of the water under discussion
key_terms.فَأْرَتَانِ: two mice that appeared in the drawn bucket
key_terms.لَا يُنَجِّسُ: does not render impure or najis
key_terms.مُرْسَلٌ: a hadith with a disconnected chain, lacking a complete isnad linkage

ai.seo_question: Does this hadith prove that water from a well remains usable after mice are found in the bucket?
ai.summary: This report describes an incident involving water drawn from a well in which mice appeared, followed by a legal analysis questioning the strength of the narration and limiting what may be inferred from it. The discussion focuses on ritual purity, the status of well water, and the caution required in deriving legal rulings from a weak or mursal hadith.
